lines.text: We can hardly fail to think of our nation as a whole. To
think of how long ago it first heard God's call and invitation
when the gospel was first preached to our forefathers, the
old Germanic tribes; and how again it was struck by the
call of God when in the sixteenth century the preaching of
Luther caused the original message of the gospel to ring out
anew. We cannot help thinking of the days when Germany
was a country dominated by the Church. Is not this shown
by the churches which belong to the whole picture of our
villages, by the minsters and cathedrals which tower up in
our towns and cities? Is it not shown by the Christian teach-
ing which moulded the minds of our youth in school and at
church? Is it not shown by church customs and festivals
which were interwoven in the very texture of our nation's
life, by holy baptism and holy marriage and church burial?
Our churches still belong essentially to the picture pre-
sented by our towns and villages; and still on Sundays peals
of bells ring out over houses and meadows. I do not propose
to enlarge on the fact that already there are villages the
focal point of whose life is no longer the church. But I must
ask: how many churches are filled Sunday by Sunday with
devout hearers of the Word? How many of our compatriots
still allow themselves to be summoned by the bells to enter
the house of God? For how many are the great cathedrals
of our cities no longer the house of God where the word of
God speaks to them and finds them, but simply artistic
monuments, an enduring product of the German mind and
civilization? What has happened to the Christian education
of youth? How many people still feel themselves seriously
bound by church discipline and obligation? We all know
that Germany is no longer a Christian country; that church
life is now only a surviving remnant, and that many desire
and hope that even this remnant will shortly disappear.
What is the reason for all this? Is it not that for so many
of us the affairs of daily life are normally more important
than the call of God? That our striving to make money, to
gain power, to enjoy the pleasures of the world, has been a
